items.prompt: Why is a 1:1 that only covers project status described as a structural waste, rather than just unhelpful?
choices: Because project status should never be discussed in any meeting

Because project status is already covered by other channels (standups, trackers, written updates) — the 1:1's distinctive value is exactly what those other channels don't surface: how someone's really doing, unescalated blockers, feedback they're sitting on, growth concerns
Because 1:1s are legally required to cover only personal topics
Because status updates take too long to discuss in any format
items.explanation: The argument isn't that status is unimportant — it's that a 1:1 spent entirely on status duplicates information already available elsewhere, wasting the one regular, private channel that could be covering things with no other reliable outlet.

items.prompt: Per L2, why does starting with the report's agenda (before the manager's items) matter structurally?
choices: It doesn't matter — agenda order has no real effect on what gets discussed

The manager already has other channels to push their own items through; starting with the report's items protects that time by construction, since manager-led items running long would otherwise squeeze out or eliminate the report's items entirely
It's purely a politeness convention with no functional purpose
Because reports are legally entitled to speak first in any meeting
items.explanation: L2's flowchart makes this explicit: manager-first structures risk the report's items being squeezed by however long the manager's list runs, while report-first structures protect that time regardless of what else needs covering afterward.

items.prompt: A report says "everything's fine" in a flat, disengaged tone, notably different from usual. Per L2, what's the appropriate response?
choices: Take the words at face value and move on, since asking further would be overstepping

Notice the mismatch between the words and the tone/energy, and gently name it ("you seem a bit off today, is everything okay?") — this isn't reading minds, it's responding to an observable signal while leaving the report in control of how much to share
Assume the worst and escalate immediately without checking in first
Ignore tone entirely, since only literal words should ever be treated as real information
items.explanation: L2 frames this as noticing a real, observable mismatch and opening a low-pressure door, not manufacturing concern or forcing disclosure — the report retains full control over how much to actually share in response.

items.prompt: Per L2, what's the trade-off between immediately answering a report's technical question and asking a coaching question first ("what have you already tried?")?
choices: There's no real trade-off; coaching questions are always strictly better

The direct answer is faster in the moment but means the next similar problem goes straight back to the manager; the coaching-first approach takes longer in this conversation but builds the report's own problem-solving capacity for next time
Coaching questions should never be used because they waste the report's time
The trade-off only applies to non-technical questions, never technical ones
items.explanation: This is a real trade-off, not a strict improvement — L2 is explicit that answer-first is faster short-term but trains the report to bring every similar problem back to the manager, while coaching-first invests conversation time now to build independent capability.

items.prompt: Per L3's first failure mode, is simply reordering the agenda (report's items first) sufficient to make a 1:1 genuinely useful?
choices: Yes — agenda order alone guarantees a useful 1:1 regardless of anything else

No — if the manager still mentally treats it as a checklist and visibly disengages once the report's items feel "resolved enough," the report notices and calibrates accordingly, defeating the structural change even though the agenda order was technically followed
No, because agenda order has no effect on the outcome either way
Yes, but only if the meeting is scheduled for at least 45 minutes
items.explanation: L3 explicitly warns that the structural fix (report-first agenda) can be undermined by an unchanged underlying mindset — genuine attentiveness throughout, not just the ordering, is what actually delivers the openness the structure is meant to create.

items.prompt: A report asks "what's our team's actual policy on requesting time off?" Per L3's second failure mode, is responding with a coaching question ("what do you think the right approach is?") appropriate here?
choices: Yes — coaching questions should be used for every question a report asks, without exception
No — this is a factual gap, not a problem-solving opportunity; over-applying coaching-mode to a request for actual information reads as evasive or as withholding help unnecessarily
Yes, because policy questions are always better handled through guided self-discovery
No, because coaching questions should never be used in any context
items.explanation: L3 explicitly distinguishes these cases: coaching questions serve problem-solving development (like the rate-limiting example), but a genuine factual gap just needs a direct, helpful answer — treating every question as a coaching opportunity misapplies the technique.
